disclaimer: This is a starting template, not legal advice. Public-records and privacy laws differ by state, and procurement rules differ by funder too. Have counsel review it before you adopt it.

questions.label: We publish or send things an AI helped write
questions.hint: Newsletters, social posts, letters, reports, website copy.

questions.label: We handle personal information
questions.hint: About residents, clients, donors, students or staff.

questions.label: We offer an AI tool the public can use
questions.hint: A chatbot, a search assistant, a form helper.

questions.label: We pay for AI by usage
questions.hint: API keys, credits, anything billed per request.

questions.label: Our AI tools connect to other systems
questions.hint: Email, shared drives, databases, calendars, automations.

questions.label: We are a government body, or speak for one
questions.hint: Cities, villages, counties, townships, districts, boards.

frameworks.name: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0
frameworks.note: Subcategory ids and titles read from the Core tables of NIST AI 100-1.
frameworks.license: Work of the U.S. Government (NIST), not subject to copyright in the United States (17 U.S.C. 105).

frameworks.name: ISO/IEC 42001:2023, AI management system
frameworks.note: The standard is paywalled. Only publicly listed clause, category and control titles are used; no requirement text was read.

rules.title: Use only approved AI tools
rules.rule: Keep one list of the AI tools your organization has approved and what each one may be used for. A new tool goes on the list before anyone uses it for work, not after.
rules.why: Tools nobody approved are tools nobody checked. You cannot protect information that flows into a service you do not know exists.
rules.manual: A shared spreadsheet with four columns: tool, approved uses, who approved it, date. Review it every quarter and remove what nobody uses.
rules.how_this_site_does_it: This site keeps a ledger of every outside service it holds a credential for. A test fails when code starts using a credential the ledger has never heard of.

mappings.outcome: Mechanisms are in place to inventory AI systems and are resourced according to organizational risk priorities.
mappings.why: Both ask for a maintained inventory of the AI systems in use, decided before use rather than after.

mappings.outcome: Resources for AI systems
mappings.why: The Resources category covers documenting the AI systems and tooling an organization relies on; the rule covers only the approved-tool list.

rules.title: Keep sensitive information out of AI tools
rules.rule: Keep personal information, case details, health, financial or law-enforcement records out of any AI tool that is not approved for that kind of information.
rules.why: What goes into a chat window may be stored, reviewed by the vendor or used to train a model. Once it is out, it is out.
rules.manual: Add a column to your approved-tools list: which kinds of information each tool may see. When in doubt, remove names and identifying details first.
rules.how_this_site_does_it: This site keeps personal details out of its public code by test: one test fails if contact details appear in the repository, and another fails if a public page imports the module that handles a client's records.

mappings.outcome: Privacy risk of the AI system – as identified in the MAP function – is examined and documented.
mappings.why: The rule keeps sensitive data out of unapproved tools, which is one way to limit the privacy risk this subcategory asks to be examined.

mappings.outcome: Use of AI systems
mappings.why: Use of AI systems covers responsible-use processes; keeping data classes out of tools is one such process.

rules.title: A person approves before AI-drafted work goes out
rules.rule: Anything an AI drafted that will be published, sent to the public or sent to another agency is read and approved by a named person first.
rules.why: AI output can be wrong, off-tone or confidently invented. The approval step is where a person takes responsibility for it.
rules.manual: Pick one approver per channel. Nothing AI-drafted is sent until the approver replies "approved" in writing, and you keep that reply.
rules.how_this_site_does_it: On this site a drafted social post can only reach "needs review", never "approved", without a person. Public-records requests are drafted by software but sent only after approval; automatic sending is off by default.

mappings.outcome: Processes for human oversight are defined, assessed, and documented in accordance with organizational policies from the GOVERN function.
mappings.why: Both require a defined, documented process for a person to oversee AI output, here an approver before anything goes out.

mappings.outcome: Policies and procedures are in place to define and differentiate roles and responsibilities for human-AI configurations and oversight of AI systems.
mappings.why: The named approver is a defined human role over AI output; the subcategory also asks for policies that differentiate human-AI configurations.

mappings.outcome: Use of AI systems
mappings.why: Use of AI systems covers responsible-use processes, of which human approval of output is one.

rules.title: Check drafts against a written list of things you never publish
rules.rule: Keep a short written list of topics and claims your organization never publishes. Check every AI-drafted piece against it before it goes out.
rules.why: An AI does not know your organization's lines unless you write them down. A list turns judgment calls into a check anyone can run.
rules.manual: Five to ten lines on one page. The approver in the previous rule checks each draft against it and says which lines were checked.
rules.how_this_site_does_it: This site runs a pre-send check against its own list in its outbound paths; a newsletter issue that trips it never sends. The list itself is kept in the code and tested for consistency.

mappings.outcome: Targeted application scope is specified and documented based on the system’s capability, established context, and AI system categorization.
mappings.why: A written never-publish list fixes the scope of what AI-drafted output may be used for.

mappings.outcome: The characteristics of trustworthy AI are integrated into organizational policies, processes, procedures, and practices.
mappings.why: The list writes the organization's own trustworthiness lines into a policy that is then checked against drafts.

mappings.outcome: Use of AI systems
mappings.why: Use of AI systems covers boundaries on intended and responsible use, of which a never-publish list is one.

rules.title: Keep public-facing AI output nonpartisan
rules.rule: AI-assisted content that speaks for a public body stays neutral on elections (candidates, parties, ballot questions) and critiques systems rather than people.
rules.why: Public bodies owe residents neutrality, and many are bound to it by law. An AI draft can slip a political frame in without anyone noticing.
rules.manual: Add a nonpartisan line to your never-publish list, and have your approver check each draft for it.
rules.how_this_site_does_it: This site's list includes a nonpartisan rule, and the same rule is written into the instructions for the AI that critiques drafts before a person sees them.

mappings.outcome: Legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood, managed, and documented.
mappings.why: Neutrality on elections is a legal duty for many public bodies; the subcategory asks that such requirements be understood and documented.

mappings.outcome: Intended purposes, potentially beneficial uses, context-specific laws, norms and expectations, and prospective settings in which the AI system will be deployed are understood and documented. Considerations include: the specific set or types of users along with their expectations; potential positive and negative impacts of system uses to individuals, communities, organizations, society, and the planet; assumptions and related limitations about AI system purposes, uses, and risks across the development or product AI lifecycle; and related TEVV and system metrics.
mappings.why: Context-specific norms and expectations for a public body are part of the deployment context this subcategory asks to be documented.

mappings.outcome: Assessing impacts of AI systems
mappings.why: Assessing impacts covers societal impact of AI systems; a nonpartisan rule guards one societal impact of public-body output.

rules.title: Say when AI is involved, and never fake a person
rules.rule: Tell people when AI wrote, summarized or answered something they rely on. Never present an AI voice, image or message as a real person.
rules.why: Trust in a public body or a nonprofit is the whole asset. Being caught passing AI off as a person spends it all at once.
rules.manual: One standard sentence on AI-assisted material, for example "Drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by staff." No AI voices or avatars that imply a real employee.
rules.how_this_site_does_it: On this site a computer reading a page aloud is labeled as a device voice, and in its language course a test keeps a synthetic voice from standing in for a native speaker.

mappings.outcome: Risks associated with transparency and accountability – as identified in the MAP function – are examined and documented.
mappings.why: Disclosing AI involvement addresses a transparency risk; the subcategory asks that such risks be examined and documented, which the rule does not require.

mappings.outcome: Organizational teams document the risks and potential impacts of the AI technology they design, develop, deploy, evaluate, and use, and they communicate about the impacts more broadly.
mappings.why: Telling people when AI is involved is communicating about the impact of AI use more broadly.

mappings.outcome: Information for interested parties of AI systems
mappings.why: Information for interested parties covers telling people they are dealing with AI and about its outputs.

rules.title: Check facts and sources before you rely on AI output
rules.rule: Before AI output is used in a decision, a publication or a reply to the public, a person checks its facts against the original source.
rules.why: AI tools produce fluent text that can be wrong. A citation you did not open is not a citation.
rules.manual: Require a source link for every factual claim in AI-assisted work, and have the approver open at least the ones that matter.
rules.how_this_site_does_it: This site's assistant attaches the sources it drew on to every answer, its civic assistant only cites approved official sites, and research figures are recomputed by test on every change.

mappings.outcome: The AI model is explained, validated, and documented, and AI system output is interpreted within its context – as identified in the MAP function – to inform responsible use and governance.
mappings.why: A person checking output against the source is interpreting AI output in context before relying on it.

mappings.outcome: Information about the AI system’s knowledge limits and how system output may be utilized and overseen by humans is documented. Documentation provides sufficient information to assist relevant AI actors when making decisions and taking subsequent actions.
mappings.why: The rule treats AI output as fallible and subject to human checking, which presupposes documented knowledge limits.

mappings.outcome: Use of AI systems
mappings.why: Use of AI systems covers responsible-use processes, of which verifying output before reliance is one.

rules.title: Put a spending cap on paid AI
rules.rule: Every paid AI service has a monthly budget, a warning before it is reached, and a stop when it is.
rules.why: Usage-based billing has no natural ceiling. A runaway automation or a busy public tool can spend a month's budget in a day.
rules.manual: Set the vendor's own billing limit and alert, name who receives the alert, and write down what gets switched off at the limit.
rules.how_this_site_does_it: This site tracks model spend month to date against a ceiling, warns at 80 percent, and pauses non-essential AI work when the ceiling is reached.

unmapped.reason: The AI RMF has no subcategory on cost or budget; a spending ceiling is financial control, not one of its trustworthiness or risk outcomes. MANAGE 2.4 was considered and rejected because it concerns performance inconsistent with intended use, not spend.
No publicly listed clause or Annex A control title is about cost limits on AI use; Resources for AI systems concerns having and documenting resources, not capping them.

rules.title: Limit how much the public can use your AI tool
rules.rule: A public AI tool has a per-person limit and a total budget, so one visitor cannot use it all or run up the bill.
rules.why: Anything free and public will be used at volume, sometimes by scripts. Limits keep the tool available and the cost predictable.
rules.manual: Use the limit settings your vendor offers, and set a separate, lower budget for the public tool than for staff use.
rules.how_this_site_does_it: This site's public assistant allows each visitor a set number of questions per minute, with further caps per hour and per day, and pauses for anonymous visitors when the monthly budget is spent.

mappings.outcome: AI system security and resilience – as identified in the MAP function – are evaluated and documented.
mappings.why: Per-person and total limits protect a public tool from abuse and exhaustion, which is part of its security and resilience.

unmapped.reason: No publicly listed clause or control title is about throttling a public AI service.

rules.title: Keep keys and passwords in one secure store
rules.rule: API keys and passwords for AI services live in one secure store. They are never pasted into documents, chat messages, AI prompts or shared screens.
rules.why: A leaked key is a bill and a breach. Keys pasted into chats and prompts end up in logs and histories you do not control.
rules.manual: Use a password manager with a shared vault for service keys. Rotate a key whenever someone who had it leaves.
rules.how_this_site_does_it: This site's setup flows read a credential on the server and write it straight to the store, so it never passes through a browser, and an audit checks that every credential in use is accounted for.

mappings.outcome: AI system security and resilience – as identified in the MAP function – are evaluated and documented.
mappings.why: Keeping keys in one secure store is a security control for the AI system and its connections.

unmapped.reason: Credential handling is an information-security control, which ISO/IEC 42001 leaves to its companion ISO/IEC 27001 rather than listing in its own Annex A.

rules.title: Give AI tools the least access they need
rules.rule: When an AI tool connects to email, files or other systems, grant only the permissions its approved use requires, and review them when the use changes.
rules.why: An AI tool with broad access can read, send or delete far more than anyone intended, and a compromised account inherits all of it.
rules.manual: Before approving a connection, write down which permissions it asks for and why each one is needed. Refuse any you cannot justify.
rules.how_this_site_does_it: This site requests only the permissions a feature uses, and a test fails if a connection ever asks for the forbidden ones.

mappings.outcome: AI system security and resilience – as identified in the MAP function – are evaluated and documented.
mappings.why: Granting only the permissions an approved use needs limits what a compromised AI connection can reach.

unmapped.reason: Access permissions are an information-security control, which ISO/IEC 42001 leaves to ISO/IEC 27001 rather than listing in its own Annex A.

rules.title: Keep an off switch anyone on duty can use
rules.rule: Every automated AI process that sends, posts or acts on your behalf can be stopped quickly by a named person, without waiting for a developer.
rules.why: When something goes wrong at night or on a weekend, the question is how fast it stops, not who built it.
rules.manual: For each automation, write one line: how to pause it and who is allowed to. Test the off switch once before relying on it.
rules.how_this_site_does_it: This site has one switch that silences every notification channel at once, each channel's starting state is a recorded owner decision, and automatic sending of records requests stays off unless someone turns it on.

mappings.outcome: Mechanisms are in place and applied, and responsibilities are assigned and understood, to supersede, disengage, or deactivate AI systems that demonstrate performance or outcomes inconsistent with intended use.
mappings.why: Both require a mechanism, with assigned responsibility, to stop an AI process that is acting outside its intended use.

mappings.outcome: Operation
mappings.why: Operation covers planning and controlling AI processes in running use; an off switch is one such control.

rules.title: Keep a record of what AI did
rules.rule: Keep a simple record of which AI tool was used, for what and by whom, with the date, for anything that leaves the organization or informs a decision.
rules.why: A records request or an audit will ask what happened. "Someone used a chatbot" is not an answer.
rules.manual: Note the tool and the reviewer in the file or ticket where the work lives. For recurring automations, keep the vendor's usage log.
rules.how_this_site_does_it: This site logs every paid AI call with what it was for and what it cost, and reads its monthly spend from that log.

mappings.outcome: The functionality and behavior of the AI system and its components – as identified in the MAP function – are monitored when in production.
mappings.why: A record of which tool did what is the raw material for monitoring AI behavior in production; the rule does not itself require the monitoring.

mappings.outcome: AI system life cycle
mappings.why: The life cycle category covers recording events from AI system operation; the rule asks for a lighter organizational record.

rules.title: Watch for automations that quietly stop working
rules.rule: Check on a schedule that each AI automation is still running and still doing its job, not only that it has not reported an error.
rules.why: The most expensive failure is the one nobody notices: a reminder that stops sending, a report that stops arriving.
rules.manual: A monthly checklist: each automation, when it last ran, and whether its output arrived. Anything that did not gets a person assigned.
rules.how_this_site_does_it: This site has a dashboard that classifies every scheduled job as fired, failing or silent, and a test keeps that list in step with the jobs that actually exist.

mappings.outcome: The functionality and behavior of the AI system and its components – as identified in the MAP function – are monitored when in production.
mappings.why: Both ask that AI functionality be checked while running in production, not only that no error was raised.

mappings.outcome: Post-deployment AI system monitoring plans are implemented, including mechanisms for capturing and evaluating input from users and other relevant AI actors, appeal and override, decommissioning, incident response, recovery, and change management.
mappings.why: A scheduled check that each automation still works is part of a post-deployment monitoring plan.

mappings.outcome: AI system operation and monitoring
mappings.why: The control is titled operation and monitoring of the AI system; the rule is the monitoring half, for automations.

mappings.outcome: Performance evaluation
mappings.why: Performance evaluation covers monitoring and measuring the management system; the rule monitors the automations it governs.

rules.title: Name an owner and review this policy on a schedule
rules.rule: One named person owns this policy. It is reviewed at least every six months and whenever you add a tool, a use or a kind of data.
rules.why: AI tools change monthly. A policy nobody owns describes last year's tools.
rules.manual: Put the owner's name and the next review date at the top of the policy, and put the review on a calendar.
rules.how_this_site_does_it: This page carries its own review date, kept in the same file as the rules, so the date and the rules change together.

mappings.outcome: Ongoing monitoring and periodic review of the risk management process and its outcomes are planned and organizational roles and responsibilities clearly defined, including determining the frequency of periodic review.
mappings.why: Both require periodic review to be planned, with the owner and the frequency defined.

mappings.outcome: Roles and responsibilities and lines of communication related to mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks are documented and are clear to individuals and teams throughout the organization.
mappings.why: Naming one policy owner documents one role; the subcategory covers roles and communication lines more widely.

mappings.outcome: Review of the AI policy
mappings.why: The control is titled review of the AI policy, which is what the rule requires, on a stated schedule.

mappings.outcome: AI roles and responsibilities
mappings.why: Naming a policy owner assigns one AI role; the control covers defining AI roles and responsibilities generally.
